Karcher Mean Thresholding for Anomaly Detection

karcher_threshold.Rd

The Karcher mean (also known as Fréchet mean or Riemannian center of mass) is a robust geometric method for setting thresholds in anomaly detection. It minimizes the sum of squared geodesic distances, making it particularly effective for data with non-Euclidean structure, heavy-tailed distributions, and extreme outliers.

Usage

set_anomaly_threshold(
  object, 
  method = "karcher",
  karcher_multiplier = 3,
  karcher_method = "complex",
  karcher_max_iter = 100,
  karcher_tol = 1e-6
)

Theory

The Karcher mean (Frechet mean) \(\mu_K\) is defined as the point that minimizes the sum of squared distances:

$$\mu_K = \arg\min_{\mu} \sum_{i=1}^{n} d^2(x_i, \mu)$$

where \(d(x_i, \mu)\) is the distance between observation \(x_i\) and the candidate mean \(\mu\).

For threshold determination, the method offers two modes:

  1. Complex mode (default): Uses KDE (kernel density estimation) weighting to account for data distribution

  2. Simple mode: Direct computation of weighted arithmetic mean

  3. Calculates scale using standard deviation (SD) of anomaly scores

  4. Sets threshold as: \(threshold = \mu_K + m \times SD\)

where \(m\) is the multiplier parameter (default: 3).

Advantages

  • Distribution awareness: Complex mode uses KDE to weight scores by their density, providing better handling of non-uniform distributions

  • Geometric optimality: Provides the optimal center (Frechet mean) in Euclidean space

  • Flexible computation: Supports both simple (fast) and complex (distribution-aware) modes

  • Proven algorithm: Based on PyOD KARCH implementation with solid empirical results

  • Theoretical foundation: Grounded in Riemannian geometry and Frechet mean theory

Comparison with Other Methods

MethodRobustnessBest For
Karcher (complex)HighNon-uniform distributions, density-aware
Karcher (simple)MediumSimple weighted mean approach
MADVery HighRobust, symmetric distributions
IQRMedium-HighBox-plot style analysis
Z-ScoreLowNormal distributions
ContaminationN/AKnown anomaly proportion

Parameters

karcher_multiplier

Controls the threshold strictness. Default: 3

  • Lower (1-2): More sensitive, detects more anomalies

  • Higher (3-4): Balanced, standard approach

  • Even higher (>4): More conservative, fewer false positives

karcher_method

Computation method. Default: "complex"

  • "complex": Uses KDE weighting for better distribution fitting

  • "simple": Direct weighted mean computation (faster)

karcher_max_iter

Maximum iterations for convergence. Default: 100

  • Increase for very complex distributions

  • Decrease for faster computation on simple data

karcher_tol

Convergence tolerance. Default: 1e-6

  • Smaller values: More precise but slower

  • Larger values: Faster but less precise

Algorithm Details

The implementation follows the PyOD KARCH approach:

Complex Mode (Default):

  1. Normalize anomaly scores to [0, 1]

  2. Generate kernel density estimation (KDE) using Gaussian kernel

  3. Perform element-wise multiplication: KDE values × sorted normalized scores

  4. Compute weighted arithmetic mean (Frechet mean in Euclidean space)

  5. Denormalize back to original scale

  6. Calculate threshold: Frechet mean + multiplier × SD

Simple Mode:

  1. Compute weighted arithmetic mean directly on scores

  2. Calculate threshold: mean + multiplier × SD

For 1D Euclidean space, the Frechet mean is simply the weighted arithmetic mean.

Computational Complexity

  • Complex mode: \(O(n \log n)\) for KDE computation

  • Simple mode: \(O(n)\) for direct mean computation

  • Space: \(O(n)\) for storing scores and KDE values

  • Complex mode is slightly slower than MAD, but provides better distribution fitting

Arguments

object

An isoForest model object

method

Set to "karcher" for this method

karcher_multiplier

Multiplier for threshold calculation (default: 3)

karcher_method

Computation method: "simple" or "complex" (default: "complex")

karcher_max_iter

Maximum iterations (default: 100)

karcher_tol

Convergence tolerance (default: 1e-6)

Value

A list containing:

threshold

The calculated threshold value

method

The method used ("karcher")

predictions

Data frame with anomaly predictions

summary

Summary statistics including Karcher mean convergence info

References

Zhao, Y., Nasrullah, Z., & Li, Z. (2019). PyOD: A Python Toolbox for Scalable Outlier Detection. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 20(96), 1-7.

Pennec, X. (2006). Intrinsic statistics on Riemannian manifolds: Basic tools for geometric measurements. Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision, 25(1), 127-154.

Afsari, B. (2011). Riemannian Lp center of mass: existence, uniqueness, and convexity. Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society, 139(2), 655-673.

Miolane, N., et al. (2020). Geomstats: A Python Package for Riemannian Geometry in Machine Learning. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 21(223), 1-9.

Examples

# Basic usage
library(isoForest)
data(iris)
model <- isoForest(iris[, 1:4])
result <- set_anomaly_threshold(model, method = "karcher")
print(result)
#> Anomaly Detection Threshold Results
#> ===================================
#> Method: karcher 
#> Threshold: 0.6244 
#> Total samples: 150 
#> Detected anomalies: 6 
#> Contamination rate: 4 %
#> Score range: [0.5468, 0.6843]
#> Score statistics:
#>   Mean: 0.5663 
#>   Median: 0.5575 
#>   SD: 0.0245 

# Tune multiplier for different sensitivity
result_sensitive <- set_anomaly_threshold(
  model, 
  method = "karcher",
  karcher_multiplier = 2.0  # More sensitive
)

result_conservative <- set_anomaly_threshold(
  model, 
  method = "karcher",
  karcher_multiplier = 4.0  # More conservative
)

# Compare simple vs complex method
result_simple <- set_anomaly_threshold(
  model,
  method = "karcher",
  karcher_method = "simple"
)

result_complex <- set_anomaly_threshold(
  model,
  method = "karcher",
  karcher_method = "complex"
)

# Compare anomaly counts
cat("Sensitive:", sum(result_sensitive$predictions$is_anomaly), "anomalies\n")
#> Sensitive: 11 anomalies
cat("Default:", sum(result$predictions$is_anomaly), "anomalies\n")
#> Default: 6 anomalies
cat("Conservative:", sum(result_conservative$predictions$is_anomaly), "anomalies\n")
#> Conservative: 4 anomalies

# Compare with other robust methods
result_mad <- set_anomaly_threshold(model, method = "mad")
result_iqr <- set_anomaly_threshold(model, method = "iqr")

comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Karcher", "MAD", "IQR"),
  Threshold = c(result$threshold, result_mad$threshold, result_iqr$threshold),
  Anomalies = c(
    sum(result$predictions$is_anomaly),
    sum(result_mad$predictions$is_anomaly),
    sum(result_iqr$predictions$is_anomaly)
  )
)
print(comparison)
#>    Method Threshold Anomalies
#> 1 Karcher 0.6244168         6
#> 2     MAD 0.5856542        19
#> 3     IQR 0.6015751        10
